The interactive example has its own motion control. Scroll inside it if you need more room.

A mathematical result for specified linked quantities

The example has two changing quantities that affect one another. Hide one line: the other line keeps the same path. Hiding the line changed the picture, not the calculation.

Now disconnect the link between them. This changes the calculation itself. The example helps explain how an unseen part can leave an effect over time. Some hidden parts leave no detectable effect; the next room explores that limit.

First hide a line. Then disconnect the link. Compare what each action changes.

Words used here
model
A simplified description used to explore a question. A result in the model needs further evidence before it describes the real world.
coupling
A link through which two parts of a model can affect one another.
Read the fuller explanation

The finite linear result begins with visible and hidden coordinates that can affect one another. Solve out the hidden part and it can return as dependence on earlier visible states and on a hidden initial condition. The reduced equation remembers what its state list no longer displays.

The small instrument here integrates two coupled coordinates. You can hide one trace while the visible evolution still depends on both. Removing the coupling is a different intervention. These operations change different things.

This is a mathematical lesson with a boundary. Some hidden sectors are exactly invisible and dynamically decoupled from the record. Their absence does not force an accessible echo. The next room keeps that harder limit in view.

Where this comes from: How the past can keep affecting a system

A mathematical result for specified linked quantities

Removing a quantity from an equation can leave an effect that depends on the past. The browser uses a smaller example to explain the idea.

Read the full source note

Hidden elimination and the quadratic memory theorem

Eliminating coupled hidden coordinates can produce a memory kernel and a term depending on their initial state. Autonomous closure requires an invariant detector kernel. The browser illustration is a two-coordinate Euler example, not a replay of the corpus certificate.
